course: Basic First Aid for Business and Community

lessons.title: CPR and AED Skills Practice
lessons.body:
When someone collapses and is not breathing, every second counts. In this lesson, you will practice CPR and using an AED on a manikin. Work on a firm, flat surface like a table or the ground. Kneel beside the manikin. Place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest, lower half of the breastbone. Put your other hand on top and interlock your fingers. Keep your arms straight and your shoulders directly above your hands. Push down hard and fast: at least 5 cm (2 inches) deep, at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. That's about 2 compressions per second. Count out loud: "One and two and three..." After 30 compressions, give 2 rescue breaths if you are trained and have a barrier device. Tilt the head back, lift the chin, pinch the nose, and blow for 1 second until the chest rises. If you are not trained or uncomfortable, do hands-only CPR: continuous chest compressions. Do not stop until help arrives or the person starts breathing.

An AED (Automated External Defibrillator) can restart the heart. Turn it on and follow the voice prompts. Expose the chest and dry it if wet. Attach the pads as shown: one below the right collarbone, one on the left side below the armpit. Make sure no one touches the person during analysis or shock. If a shock is advised, press the flashing button. Then immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes before the AED reanalyzes. In Africa, AEDs are found in airports, large malls, and some offices. If you don't have one, continue CPR until the ambulance arrives. Practice switching compressors every 2 minutes to avoid fatigue. Use a metronome app or a song like "Stayin' Alive" to keep the right rhythm. Remember: for children, use one hand and push about 5 cm deep; for infants, use two fingers and push 4 cm deep. Always check for breathing and pulse for no more than 10 seconds before starting.

lessons.title: Choking Relief Skills Practice
lessons.body:
Choking happens when an object blocks the airway. The person may clutch their throat, cough weakly, or make a high-pitched noise. If they can cough forcefully, encourage them to keep coughing. If they cannot breathe, speak, or cough, act immediately. For a conscious adult or child, stand behind them and give 5 back blows. Use the heel of your hand to strike between the shoulder blades. Then give 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver). Stand behind, wrap your arms around their waist, make a fist with one hand, place it just above the navel, and grab it with your other hand. Pull inward and upward sharply. Repeat 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or they become unconscious. If they become unconscious, lower them to the ground and start CPR.

For a choking infant (under 1 year), sit and place the infant face-down along your forearm, supporting the head. Give 5 back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. Then turn the infant face-up and give 5 chest thrusts using two fingers on the center of the chest. Repeat until the object is expelled. Do not do abdominal thrusts on infants.

For pregnant women or very large people, use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts. Stand behind, place your arms under their armpits, and give thrusts to the center of the chest. If you are alone and choking, you can give yourself abdominal thrusts with your own fist, or press your upper abdomen against a chair back or table edge. Practice on a manikin or a partner (with caution) to build muscle memory. In many African communities, people may try to give water or oil to a choking personânever do that; it can make things worse. Also, avoid blind finger sweeps in the mouth; you might push the object deeper. Only remove the object if you can see it. After successful choking relief, the person should still be checked by a health worker because internal injuries can occur.

lessons.title: Bleeding Control and Bandaging Practice
lessons.body:
Severe bleeding can kill in minutes. Your first step is to ensure your own safety: wear gloves if available, or use a plastic bag as a barrier. For heavy bleeding, apply direct pressure with a clean cloth, gauze, or even a shirt. Press hard and do not lift to check. If blood soaks through, add more layers on topâdo not remove the first layer. Maintain pressure for at least 5 minutes. If bleeding is on an arm or leg and does not stop, you can apply a tourniquet. Use a commercial tourniquet if available, or a wide strip of cloth (at least 5 cm wide) and a stick to tighten. Place it 5-7 cm above the wound, not on a joint. Tighten until bleeding stops. Note the time. Do not loosen it; that's for medical staff.

For smaller cuts, clean the wound with clean water and mild soap. Apply antibiotic ointment if available. Cover with a sterile bandage or clean cloth. For bandaging, use a roller bandage. Start below the wound and wrap upward, overlapping each turn by half. Do not wrap too tightâyou should be able to slip a finger under the bandage. Check for circulation: press a nail bed; it should turn pink within 2 seconds. If fingers or toes are cold, blue, or numb, loosen the bandage. For a wound on the head, use a triangular bandage as a cap. For a wound on the palm, place a roll of gauze in the hand and wrap the fingers around it. For a wound on the elbow or knee, bandage in a bent position. Practice on a partner or a manikin. In rural Africa, you may not have sterile supplies. Use the cleanest cloth you can find and boil it if possible. After bandaging, always wash your hands. If the wound is deep, dirty, or from an animal bite, seek medical care for tetanus shot and possible rabies prevention.

lessons.title: Splinting and Immobilization Practice
lessons.body:
A fracture is a broken bone. You may see deformity, swelling, or hear a snap. Do not try to push the bone back. Your goal is to immobilize the area to prevent further injury. For a broken arm, use a splint that extends from above the elbow to beyond the wrist. You can use a rolled newspaper, a piece of wood, or a sturdy stick. Pad the splint with cloth to avoid pressure sores. Place the splint on the injured side and secure it with bandages or strips of cloth at three points: above the break, below the break, and at the joint. Then use a sling to support the arm. For a sling, use a triangular bandage or a large cloth. Place the arm across the chest, tie the ends behind the neck, and knot at the elbow.

For a broken leg, do not move the person unless absolutely necessary. Immobilize the leg by tying it to the other leg (the unaffected one) using bandages or cloths at the ankles, knees, and thighs. If you have a splint, place it on the outside of the leg from the armpit to the foot. Secure it at the chest, waist, knee, and ankle. For a broken collarbone, use a sling and a swathe (a wide bandage wrapped around the chest and arm) to keep the arm from moving. For a broken finger, tape it to the next finger with a small piece of cloth or tape, but not too tight. For a broken rib, do not wrap the chest; instead, have the person hold a pillow against the ribs for support. Always check circulation after splinting: press the nail bed and see if it turns pink quickly. If not, loosen the splint. In Africa, traditional bonesetters are common, but improper setting can cause permanent disability. Always encourage the person to go to a clinic or hospital for an X-ray. Practice splinting on a partner using everyday materials. Remember: when in doubt, immobilize and seek help.

lessons.title: Scenario-Based Emergency Simulations
lessons.body:
In this lesson, you will practice responding to realistic emergencies. Work in groups of 3-4: one person is the victim, one is the rescuer, and others are observers who give feedback. Use a timer and a manikin or a willing volunteer. Scenario 1: A man collapses in a shop. He is unresponsive and not breathing. You check the scene for safety, tap his shoulders, and shout, "Are you okay?" No response. You call for help and ask someone to call an ambulance and get an AED. You start CPR with 30 compressions and 2 breaths. After 2 minutes, the AED arrives. You apply it and follow prompts. Continue until help arrives. Debrief: Did you check for breathing? Did you compress deep enough?

Scenario 2: A child chokes on a groundnut. She is coughing weakly and turning blue. You give 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts. The groundnut pops out. She starts crying. You comfort her and advise her parents to take her to a clinic. Scenario 3: A farmer cuts his leg with a machete. Blood is spurting. You put on gloves, apply direct pressure with a clean cloth, and elevate the leg. Bleeding slows. You bandage the wound and check circulation. You note the time and advise him to go to a health center for stitches.

Scenario 4: A woman falls from a bicycle and has a deformed forearm. You do not move her. You check for other injuries. You splint the arm with a rolled magazine and a sling. You monitor her breathing and keep her warm. You call for transport. After each scenario, discuss what went well and what could be improved. Use a checklist: Did you ensure scene safety? Did you call for help? Did you use correct technique? Did you show empathy? Practice until you can perform each skill without hesitation. In real life, you may be the only person who knows first aid. These simulations build confidence and speed. Do them monthly with your colleagues or community group. Remember: in Africa, help may take time to arrive, so your actions in the first 10 minutes are critical.

lessons.title: Final Skills Assessment and Certification
lessons.body:
To earn your Basic First Aid certification, you must pass a skills assessment. This is a hands-on test where an instructor watches you perform key skills. You will be evaluated on CPR, choking relief, bleeding control, and splinting. For CPR, you must show correct hand placement, depth (at least 5 cm), rate (100-120 per minute), and use of an AED. You will do 2 minutes of CPR on a manikin. For choking, you will demonstrate back blows and abdominal thrusts on a manikin. For bleeding, you will apply direct pressure and a bandage. For splinting, you will immobilize a broken arm with a splint and sling. You must also answer 10 oral questions about when to call for help, signs of shock, and how to prevent infection.

The assessment takes about 30 minutes. You need to score at least 80% to pass. If you don't pass, you can retake it after one week of practice. Upon passing, you will receive a certificate valid for 2 years. Keep it in your business or community health post. To maintain your skills, practice monthly and consider taking a refresher course every year. In many African countries, first aid certification is recognized by the Red Cross and St. John Ambulance. You can also join a local first aid club. After certification, you can train others in your community. Start by teaching simple skills like handwashing and bleeding control. Remember: certification is just the beginning. Real confidence comes from regular practice. Set up a monthly drill with your coworkers. Use the same scenarios from Lesson 5. Keep your first aid kit stocked and check expiration dates. Your ability to act calmly and correctly can save a lifeâmaybe even someone you love.

quiz.q: What is the correct rate for adult chest compressions during CPR?
quiz.explanation: The recommended rate is 100-120 compressions per minute to maintain blood flow.

quiz.q: How deep should you push when doing CPR on an adult?
quiz.explanation: Adult chest compressions should be at least 5 cm deep to be effective.

quiz.q: When using an AED, where should you place the pads?
options: A) One on the chest, one on the back
B) One below the right collarbone, one on the left side below the armpit
C) Both on the upper chest
D) One on the abdomen, one on the chest
quiz.explanation: This placement allows the shock to travel through the heart.

quiz.q: What should you do if a choking adult can cough forcefully?
options: B) Encourage them to keep coughing
quiz.explanation: A forceful cough is effective at expelling the object; thrusts could worsen the blockage.

quiz.q: How many back blows and abdominal thrusts do you give to a choking adult?
quiz.explanation: The cycle is 5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts, repeated until the object is out.

quiz.q: For a choking infant, what technique should you use?
options: B) Back blows and chest thrusts
quiz.explanation: Infants receive 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts.

quiz.q: What is the first step when you see someone bleeding heavily?
options: B) Put on gloves or use a barrier
D) Clean the wound with water
quiz.explanation: Protecting yourself from bloodborne diseases is the priority before providing care.

quiz.q: How long should you apply direct pressure to a bleeding wound before checking?
quiz.explanation: Pressure must be maintained for at least 5 minutes to allow clotting.

quiz.q: Where should a tourniquet be placed?
quiz.explanation: Placing it 5-7 cm above the wound and not on a joint is most effective.

quiz.q: What should you do if a bandage is too tight?
options: C) Add more bandage on top
quiz.explanation: A too-tight bandage can cut off circulation; loosen it to restore blood flow.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of splinting a fracture?
quiz.explanation: Splinting prevents movement of the broken bone to avoid further injury.

quiz.q: For a broken arm, where should the splint extend?
options: B) From above the elbow to beyond the wrist
quiz.explanation: The splint must immobilize the joints above and below the fracture.

quiz.q: How do you check circulation after splinting?
options: B) Press a nail bed and see if it turns pink within 2 seconds
quiz.explanation: Capillary refill is a quick way to assess circulation.

quiz.q: What should you do for a suspected broken leg if you must move the person?
options: B) Immobilize the leg to the other leg
quiz.explanation: Tying the injured leg to the unaffected leg provides stability.

quiz.q: In a scenario simulation, what is the first thing you should do?
options: B) Check the scene for safety
quiz.explanation: Ensuring scene safety prevents you from becoming a victim.

quiz.q: After 2 minutes of CPR, what should you do if an AED arrives?
options: B) Apply the AED and follow prompts
quiz.explanation: The AED should be used as soon as it is available to analyze the heart rhythm.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when helping a choking person?
quiz.explanation: Giving water can worsen the blockage and should never be done.

quiz.q: What should you do after successful choking relief?
options: B) Advise them to see a health worker
quiz.explanation: Internal injuries may have occurred, so medical evaluation is recommended.

quiz.q: For a bleeding wound on the palm, how should you bandage it?
options: A) Wrap tightly around the fingers
B) Place a roll of gauze in the hand and wrap fingers around it
C) Use a triangular bandage as a cap
quiz.explanation: This technique keeps the hand in a functional position and applies pressure.

quiz.q: What is the minimum score to pass the final skills assessment?
quiz.explanation: 80% is required to demonstrate competency in all skills.

quiz.q: How long is the first aid certification valid?
quiz.explanation: Certification is typically valid for 2 years, after which a refresher is needed.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are alone and choking?
quiz.explanation: Self-administered abdominal thrusts or using a chair back can dislodge the object.

quiz.q: When should you not use abdominal thrusts?
quiz.explanation: For pregnant women, chest thrusts are used instead to avoid harm to the fetus.

quiz.q: What is the correct compression depth for a child during CPR?
quiz.explanation: For children, compress about 5 cm (2 inches) using one or two hands.

quiz.q: What should you do if a wound is bleeding through the first bandage?
options: B) Add more layers on top
quiz.explanation: Removing the bandage can disrupt clot formation; add more layers and maintain pressure.

quiz.q: For a broken collarbone, what should you use?
options: A) A splint on the arm
quiz.explanation: A sling supports the arm, and a swathe wraps around the chest to keep it still.

quiz.q: What is the correct action for a choking infant who becomes unconscious?
quiz.explanation: If the infant becomes unresponsive, begin CPR immediately.

quiz.q: How often should you practice your first aid skills after certification?
quiz.explanation: Monthly practice maintains muscle memory and confidence.

quiz.q: What should you include in a first aid kit for bleeding control?
options: B) Gloves, gauze, bandages, and tape
quiz.explanation: A comprehensive kit includes barriers, dressings, and supplies to control bleeding.

quiz.q: Why is it important to note the time when applying a tourniquet?
options: A) To know when to loosen it
quiz.explanation: Medical staff need to know how long the tourniquet has been applied to assess tissue damage.
